Foreword by Andrew Forzani, Government Chief Commercial Officer and Sam Ulyatt, Chief Executive Officer of the Government Commercial Agency

Consultancy firms are a valuable asset that can bring expertise to the public sector, as evidenced by major government projects that have been supported by consultants.

The Civil Service must ensure that we maximise the value generated through consultancy engagements, by setting up our procurements for success, building effective relationships with suppliers, and by considering how to develop longer-term Civil Service capability via knowledge and skills transfer.

In July 2024, the Government set targets aimed at halving Central Government consultancy spending. The refreshed Consultancy Playbook addresses how we can work towards this with updated guidance on:

expanded definitions of different types of extended workforce, to ensure we select the right type for our needs, and to categorise, declare and report this spend accurately

a range of internal Civil Service teams, who can provide consultancy-style services or support the procurement of extended workforce

the effect of Artificial Intelligence on the world of consultancy, and how we can best position ourselves to embrace this

the role of the Procurement Act 2023, particularly in preliminary market engagement and award criteria

On the 1st of April 2026, the Government Commercial Agency (GCA) was created, which combined the former Crown Commercial Services, and key teams in the Government Commercial Function, including Markets, Sourcing and the Complex Transactions Team.

The GCA hosts over 100 commercial agreements, and aims to improve how the public sector procures goods and services, including consultancy and other extended workforce services. Throughout the Playbook, we recommend that public sector organisations contact the GCA PROfessional Services Procurement Efficiency

Resourcing team (PROSPER) for guidance and support when going to market and help you maximise value.

By adopting this refreshed Playbook, alongside our range of other commercial Playbooks, contracting authorities can ensure to get things right at the start, maximising value for money and driving Civil Service self-sufficiency and capability.

As the Chief Commercial Officer for the Government Commercial Function and Non-Executive Chair of the GCA, and the Chief Executive Officer for the GCA, we are delighted to support the launch of the Consultancy Playbook V2.0 and look forward to seeing its principles drive commercial excellence across government and create value for the nation.

Andrew Forzani, Chief Commercial Officer for the Government Commercial Function and Non-Executive Chair of the GCA

Sam Ulyatt, Chief Executive Officer for the GCA

Introduction

Considering when and how to use consultancy services effectively is vital to the success of our projects and services. Version 2.0 of the Consultancy Playbook remains focused on getting consultancy engagements right at the start, by ensuring that contracting authorities are using the correct external resources in the right instances to fill specific skills and knowledge gaps which can not be filled by internal staff or resources from across the public sector.

In July 2024, the Government made a commitment to halve consultancy spending. To support this aim, departments have been asked to bring in the following internal controls on consultancy and professional services. The controls are as follows:

spend over £600,000, or contracts with a duration of over 9 months require Ministerial approval

spend over £100,000, or contracts with a duration of over 3 months require relevant Accounting Officer approval

There may be legitimate exceptions of some sub-categories of this control (e.g. legal services or spending on cross-government support) which Accounting Officers should decide on. A well trained and skilled Civil Service needs to be disciplined in its use of external consultants. Although, there will always be requirements for specialist skills that the Civil Service doesn’t possess, you should ensure that sufficient attention is given both to the successful delivery of external consultancy projects and to effective knowledge transfer so that internal capability continue to grow. This approach will deliver value for money as well as better quality projects and public services for the citizens that use and rely on them.

By following this guidance you can expect to:

understand when consultants can add the most value

set your procurements up for success

achieve more favourable outcomes when going to market

be a more effective client of consultants while building meaningful relationships with our suppliers

improve Civil Service capability by maximising knowledge generation and knowledge and skills transfer across the contract life cycle

take advantage of the full range and diversity of consultancies and other extended workforce providers available in the marketplace, including SMEs and VCSEs

Version 2.0 of the Playbook was developed by the Government Commercial Agency’s Markets, Sourcing and Suppliers team, with input from industry stakeholders and public officials, from across commercial, finance, human resources (HR) and workforce planning as part of the wider consultancy reform agenda to transform how government procures and uses consultancy.

Key terms and scope

Department – refers to any central government department or arm’s length body (ALB).

Contracting authority – refers to any public sector organisation. This could include, for example, a central government department or local authority.

Should – indicates a principle or policy requirement to be implemented on a ‘comply or explain’ basis by Departments.

Shall or must – indicates a legislative requirement that must be complied with.

- there is more transparency on actual value delivered by consultants;

- we are prepared for more mature contract management (otherwise issues related to the achievement of results and associated rewards may arise).

No pricing mechanism is risk free, it is good practice to trial the use of your commercial evaluation to see if abnormal low tenders alter the outcome and exposes you to additional risks. Where you evaluate the average rate card against levels of seniority, some suppliers may choose to price certain rates as low as £1. You should interrogate any low cost bid as per your organisation’s process and note the provisions on dealing with abnormally low tenders in section 19 the PA 23.

Evaluating bids

The bid evaluation process should work so that suppliers are able to put forward their best bid and clients can effectively evaluate these to ensure the best solution is chosen. When evaluating bids, ensure that:

the project team who will be working alongside the consultants are involved in the evaluation process, as well as commercial and finance. This will help to ensure that bids are evaluated compliantly, and in line with project priorities. Refer to the OKUA model on page 9 to ensure that the relevant functions have been considered

evaluators have the skills necessary to evaluate a bid effectively. For example, those performing the price evaluation should have the necessary financial skills

you are aware that if using a competitive tendering procedure under PA 23, contracting authorities must assess bids to identify and award the contract to the supplier with the ‘most advantageous tender’ (unless it chooses to abandon or cancel the procurement).

evaluators should satisfy themselves that the consultant team proposed in the bid will be the team that ends up working on the engagement. It should not be the case that we are offered one team, but then a different and potentially less suitable team arrives when the engagement gets underway

you consider using presentations and interviews as part of the tendering procedure as they can help you understand how consultants work and whether the consultant team will be a good match for the Civil Service team. The guidance on page 40 details how best to use presentations and interviews in evaluation

the project team provides structured feedback to suppliers at the end of the evaluation period. This will improve the consultancy ecosystem by enabling suppliers to put forward stronger bids in future. This should be supported by notes and feedback produced by evaluators when assessing bids

When using interviews or presentations contracting authorities should ensure:

the ITT clearly explains the process for deciding which bidders take part;

there is a standard script and marking scheme;

presentations and interviews are only used to either evidence the written bid or to evaluate the skills / experience of the particular people who will be delivering the contract. They should not be used to cover selection stage criteria (e.g. past performance, supplier identity, etc.);

scoring methodologies are objective;

presentations and interviews are permitted by the framework agreement and used in accordance with the process set out in the framework agreement.

Understanding spend data

Contracting authorities should be capturing and maintaining accurate data about our use of extended workforce services. This includes the suppliers used and their size, the type of extended workforce, the cost and the reasons why external resources are being used. Having such data allows the government to:

build a picture of the government’s extended workforce ecosystem, and understand the impact of ongoing drives to reduce unnecessary consultancy spend

identify potential synergies and avoid duplication

gain insight into skills and knowledge gaps to strengthen internal capability and facilitate cross-government knowledge sharing

There is no official rule on how much consultancy can form part of a requirement, but it is commonplace for consultancy to be in addition to the delivery or implementation of the advice. Contracting authorities should be mindful that the workers remain outside of the organisational structure and the work remains under the supervision, direction and control of the supplier.

Departments are required to report consultancy and contingent labour spending in their Annual Report and Accounts and thus it is important that spending is accurately categorised in internal systems. Contracting authorities should follow the process map below to ensure we are capturing the right data effectively.

Approach to data input and capture

1.Are the services consultancy?

First consider whether the services being supplied are in fact consultancy. As mentioned in Table 1 and Annex 1 there are various types of extended workforce, which includes contingent labour, professional services and resource augmentation.

2. What type of consultancy?

If it is consultancy, identify its specific type, such as strategy, or project portfolio management. If you are unsure then ask for support from commercial colleagues with expertise in consultancy. Where invoices contain a mix of services, the invoice should be classified as the area with the majority of spend.

3. Applying for internal consultancy spend approval

The Government has made a commitment to halve consultancy spending. To support this aim, departments have been asked to bring in the following internal controls on consultancy and professional services. The controls are as follows:

spend over £100,000, or contracts with a duration of over 3 months require relevant Accounting Officer approval

Setting procurements up for success

Consultancy services should only be used in exceptional circumstances to fill specific skills and knowledge gaps that can’t be provided by internal resources. However, if you decide that commissioning external consultants is the most effective delivery model for your business need, it is essential that you set the procurement up for success.

Getting things right at the start will save time downstream, deliver greater value for money and help to build stronger relationships with suppliers. You should consider the following principles right at the start of consultancy procurements, to self-evaluate requests for consultancy and ensure that you’re setting up for success. You should:

have a clear understanding of the overall project outcomes, as this will allow you to specify the deliverables for the engagement

establish the sector you need support from (like strategy, finance, or IT) and the type of extended workforce which would be appropriate, such as pure consultancy (advisory) services, professional services, or resource augmentation

ensure that project teams engage appropriately with commercial (including GCA where appropriate), finance and legal functions right at the start of procurements. This will ensure stakeholders are fully aligned, that the procurement is compliant with regulation and delivers value for money

decide how to incorporate and incentivise knowledge generation, knowledge and skills transfer, and sharing across the contract lifecycle to build internal capability, particularly if there is a significant capability issue and this is a long-term requirement, to reduce the need to buy the same skills and knowledge again

have a firm grasp of our intended governance structures and ways of working, including SRO responsibilities, and escalation procedures

These factors are often interlinked and are likely to impact the way you procure and manage consultancy services. For example, the approach to a complex multi-year digital transformation programme will differ from a short and quick piece of strategic advice. Proportionality is key, and you should always consider basic criteria such as the value, duration and scope of the engagement to ensure a suitable approach.

Considering scope and scale

Consider SMEs and VCSEs: Lotting

The Procurement Act (PA 23) mandates that contracting authorities have the duty to consider lots. Before publishing a tender notice they must undergo this process. If the contracts can be awarded via lotting this must be arranged, or a reason will need to be provided.

Break down large mixed requirements into suitable Lots to ensure needs are well matched to firms’ expertise and to ensure we are facilitating access for suppliers of all sizes.

This helps to avoid over-reliance on one firm and taps into the most relevant expertise, and allows the government to plan to transition to internal capacity at the right time.

When deciding on suitable lots of requirements, ensure that this is done to best match the expertise of firms, and not to avoid control thresholds.

Consultancy engagements should be time-limited with clearly defined deliverables and outputs, and disaggregated appropriately. If contracting authorities are considering putting in place longer term contracting models, such as overarching contracts or delivery partner arrangements with defined call-off procedures, the guidance below should be followed:

Using umbrella contracts or delivery partner arrangements

When considering putting in place overarching contracts or delivery partner arrangements, ensure that:

you clearly understand both the capability and capacity gaps faced – external consultants should be used to fill specific capability gaps, rather than capacity shortages, which are better suited to contingent labour;

you consider the most effective delivery model – GCA PROSPER can provide guidance on this, and can be contacted via prosper@gca.gov.uk;

individual work packages are specific to the engagement and are directly linked to the deliverables in the specification;

you apply governance to individual work packages from these arrangements – this includes exploring internal options, ensuring that knowledge transfer is being prioritised, and that any spend control requirements are being followed prior to calling-off from the contract;

you maintain commercial tension when using these arrangements – by undertaking regular benchmarking of rates, and market testing for new requirements, to assess their value.

Engaging with the market

Talking to the market is one of the most important things you can do. Conducting preliminary market engagement before launching a tender can be hugely beneficial to not only inform suppliers of any upcoming opportunities, but to use market knowledge and expertise to help shape your requirements. Ensuring that potential suppliers

have an in-depth understanding of your requirements and sufficient time to create an innovative bid should promote better bids and reduce clarification questions which can lengthen timescales.

Preliminary market engagement can also assist contracting authorities with the following:

selecting the route to market, and the relevant conditions of participation and award criteria

preparing the tender notice and other tender documentation

identifying potential appropriate suppliers for the requirement

identifying likely contractual terms

building capacity amongst relevant suppliers in relation to contract award
